name: Daria Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven at Oak Hollow, feeding the pigs, twenty-odd of them, and collecting eggs from the mobile hen house. Then it's the market garden: weeding, picking, washing and packing veg boxes for the Thursday round. I'm still slow, and I've killed more seedlings than I'd like to admit. But I'm outside, I'm moving, and nobody is timing my calls.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did twenty-two years in a call centre for an insurance company. Last year they replaced most of us with an AI voice system, the kind that talks back to customers like a person. I was 56, Jo said go and do the thing you always talked about, so I knocked on the door of Sam and Priya, the young couple who run Oak Hollow. The pay is the lowest I've ever had and Jo's library hours got cut too, so we've got about two weeks of money in the bank at any time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you get on with technology on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the odd one, I'm the 58-year-old who's better with it than the 30-year-olds. I use an AI app every day: it tells me what a weed is from a photo, it helps me write the box newsletter, and I've got it keeping the pig weights in a spreadsheet. Sam laughs at me but he's started asking me to look things up for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. So the thing that took my old job was the high point? That's almost funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd post something cheeky online, like: turns out it only came for the call centres. My old team has a group chat and we'd have a bitter laugh about it. At Oak Hollow I'd say good, now let's use it properly instead of being scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I made the right move. I'm somewhere it can't touch, doing work I like, and the little bits of AI I use make me a bit faster. The problem is still the money. A plateau doesn't put anything in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep pushing my little tools. I'd ask Sam and Priya if I could take over the box scheme orders and the online shop, because I'm already half doing it, and maybe that's worth a bit more per hour. I'd try to get a month of money saved, which we've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit smug if I'm honest. I jumped and landed on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a plateau doesn't put anything in the bank. What would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being paid for what I'm actually doing. Right now I'm paid as a farm hand and I'm also doing the office work they used to do at midnight. If they paid me for the office half, Jo and I could stop checking the balance before every shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the call centre experience come in useful on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than I thought. When a box customer rings up furious about slugs in their lettuce, Sam goes pale and hands me the phone. Twenty-two years of angry people about car insurance, a slug is nothing.

S0.say: I'd post a cheeky line that it only came for the call centres, and laugh with my old team. At the farm I'd say now let's use it properly instead of being scared.
S0.think: It means I made the right move: I'm somewhere it can't touch and my AI tools make me faster. But a plateau doesn't put anything in the bank.
S0.do: Keeps working and asks the owners to let her run the box scheme orders and online shop for better pay. Tries to save a full month of expenses for the first time.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug that she jumped and landed on her feet.
S0.quote: Twenty-two years of angry people about car insurance, a slug is nothing.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is the rare older worker who is the most tech-confident person on her farm, using an AI app daily. She was already replaced once by AI, and this picture felt like vindication. Her real issue is pay: she does office work on a farm hand's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, this is the one I believe. It's already what happened to me, just spreading out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that the people who lose jobs need proper help, real retraining with pay while you learn, not a link to an online course. When I was let go we got a leaflet. I'd say that online and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I think this is good news, strangely. Oak Hollow is small, nobody's buying a weeding robot for two acres any time soon, and I'm the one who'd know how to bring in the useful bits. I've already been through the worst version of this once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start reading about the small robots, the solar weeders and the camera hen counters, and show Sam and Priya which ones make sense for a farm our size. I'd offer to run them if we got one. I'd also volunteer at the local unemployed centre to help people from my old call centre learn the tools, because nobody helped us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little sore, remembering how it was the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody helped you the first time. What would have helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months of pay while I learned something, and someone sitting next to me, not a website. I had to teach myself all this on my phone on the bus, at 56. Jo held my hand through the worst of it, and she shouldn't have had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would bringing machines into Oak Hollow put anyone else's work at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. There's Kev, who comes in three days a week to do the heavy digging and fencing. If a robot did the weeding it would free me up, not him, but I'd be lying if I said I hadn't thought about it. I'd want Sam and Priya to promise Kev's days first.

S1.say: I'd say people losing jobs need real retraining with pay while they learn, not a link to an online course. When I was let go we got a leaflet.
S1.think: For me this is oddly good news: the farm is small and I'm the one who'd know how to bring in the useful tools. I've already lived through the worst version once.
S1.do: Researches small robots like solar weeders and shows the owners which suit their farm, offering to run them. Volunteers at the local unemployed centre to teach former call centre staff to use AI tools.
S1.feel: Mostly fine, with a sore memory of the first time she was replaced.
S1.quote: I had to teach myself all this on my phone on the bus, at 56.
S1.fieldNote: Daria sees slow change as her opportunity, because she'd become the person who brings in and runs the machines. Her progressive views showed in her demand for paid retraining and in volunteering to help others. When pressed, she admitted a new machine could threaten a colleague's days and wanted him protected first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Two years. No, that's different. That's the call centre again, but for everyone at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be very loud. I'd say the companies that build this should pay for a basic income for everyone, starting the day it arrives, and I'd organise people from my old team and the farm round here to say so. I'd post every day, write to the papers, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the trick doesn't work twice. The first time a computer took my job, I ran to the fields. With this one there's no field left to run to. I've got two weeks of money and I'm 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a group straight away, farmworkers and ex-call-centre people, and get us into the farmworkers' union as a bloc. I'd try to make something on the side that's about people, not tasks, maybe running AI help sessions for older folk in the village hall, small money but something. Once it arrived I'd sign on for every bit of support going and so would Jo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry under it. I did the brave thing once and it bought me two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does that make you feel better placed than others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about a week. Knowing how to use it is useful while there's a person needed to use it. If it can do the whole farm, my skill is knowing how to talk to the thing that replaces me. That's not a job, that's a nice hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only having two years' warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It kills the plan. My plan was to grow into the office side at Oak Hollow over five, six years and leave at 66 having been useful. Two years means I'm 60 and on the street, with Jo's hours already cut. There's no time to save anything when you've never had a month in the bank.

S2.say: I'd say the companies building this should pay for a basic income for everyone from day one. I'd organise my old team and local farmworkers and post every day.
S2.think: The trick doesn't work twice: I ran to the fields last time, and now there's nowhere left to run. I'd be 60 with two weeks of money.
S2.do: Starts a group of farmworkers and former call centre workers and brings them into the union together. Runs paid AI help sessions for older villagers on the side, then signs on for all available support once it arrives.
S2.feel: Frightened, with anger underneath that her brave move only bought two years.
S2.quote: The first time a computer took my job, I ran to the fields. With this one there's no field left to run to.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI broke Daria's whole story about herself, that she outran the machines by moving to the land. Her tech skills felt worthless once a machine could do everything. She'd turn her fear into organising, which fits her progressive views, but money is the hard limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63. Okay. That gives me time to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly the same: a basic income paid for by the companies, and paid retraining now, not after. I'd say five years is long enough that there's no excuse if government isn't ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to build something. I could be the person in this valley who helps small farms set up the robots, while that's still a job. It wouldn't last forever, but it might last to 66 if I'm quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a short course on farm robotics if I could find one that's free or cheap, and I'd ask Sam and Priya to let Oak Hollow be a test farm for something small. I'd charge other small farms for an afternoon of setting up their apps and machines. Every bit of that extra money goes straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but busy, which suits me better than nervous and stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you need money to get started on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, and that's the catch. A decent laptop, petrol to get round the farms, maybe a course fee. I'd probably sell my mum's old sewing machine, it's worth a few hundred, and ask my eldest for a loan I'd actually pay back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'm a victim. With five, I'm a bit of a guide. It's a short window, but it's a window, and I'd climb through it.

S3.say: I'd keep calling for a basic income paid for by the companies and paid retraining now. Five years is long enough that government has no excuse.
S3.think: Five years is enough to build something: I could help small farms in the valley set up robots while that's still a job. It might last until 66 if I'm quick.
S3.do: Takes a cheap or free short course on farm robotics and asks the owners to trial a small machine. Charges other small farms for setting up apps and machines, funding it by selling an old sewing machine and a loan from her son, and saves the extra.
S3.feel: Nervous but busy, which suits her better than nervous and stuck.
S3.quote: With two, I'm a victim. With five, I'm a bit of a guide.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turned Daria from victim to entrepreneur almost instantly: she'd sell set-up help to small farms. She was realistic that it only lasts until the machines can set themselves up. The startup money would come from selling a family heirloom and a loan from her son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68. I'd have done my bit and got out by then, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one to get right, because there's time to plan. I'd push for rules on what robots can do on farms, a fund for retraining and a basic income ready to switch on. I'd keep pushing at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly fine. I'd get to my pension at 66 and spend the last years helping Oak Hollow set up. My worry is the young ones, and the people my age who aren't comfortable with this stuff and won't have a Jo at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course, help Oak Hollow bring in machines bit by bit, and keep the side work going with other farms. I'd save properly, finally. And I'd keep running the help sessions at the village hall, because that's the bit I'd be proudest of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, honestly. A bit tired at the thought, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the people your age you're thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, for one. He's 59, he can build a fence you could lean a bus on, and he's never sent an email. Ten years is enough to get him through, but only if someone sits with him. That someone might have to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will waste the ten years. Everyone will say we've got time, and then it'll be 2034 and we'll be where I was in 2025, holding a leaflet.

S4.say: I'd say this is the one to get right because there's time: rules for farm robots, a retraining fund and a basic income ready to switch on.
S4.think: It's mostly fine for me because I'd reach my pension first. I worry for the young and for people my age who aren't comfortable with technology.
S4.do: Takes the robotics course and helps the farm bring in machines gradually while keeping up side work with other farms. Saves properly and keeps running AI help sessions in the village hall.
S4.feel: Hopeful, though a bit tired at the thought of it.
S4.quote: Everyone will say we've got time, and then it'll be 2034 and we'll be where I was in 2025, holding a leaflet.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Daria relaxed about herself and turned to others, especially her colleague Kev, who has never sent an email. Her one worry is that society wastes the warning time. She rated this picture as hopeful, yet still felt uneasy about everyone else.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away the one thing I'm good at, which is seeing it coming and moving first. What would help is a basic income that starts automatically, so you don't have to beg for it, and paid retraining with a real person, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked what it's like to be the old person who's good with the new stuff. It's lonely. The young ones think I'm a novelty and the people my age think I've gone over to the other side.

headlineQuote: I'm the 58-year-old who's better with it than the 30-year-olds.
portrait: Daria Weber is 58 and spent twenty-two years in an insurance call centre until an AI voice system replaced most of the staff in 2025. She now feeds pigs, collects eggs and packs veg boxes at Oak Hollow, a small farm run by a young couple, earning the lowest wage of her life. She uses an AI app every day and is quietly running the farm's office side. She's progressive and wants companies to fund a basic income and paid retraining. Slow change and a ten-year AGI look like chances to her, but AGI in two years would mean her escape to the land only bought her time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it takes away her one strength, seeing change coming and moving first, and leaves her at 60 with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that starts automatically, without having to beg for it, and paid retraining with a real person beside you.
